PVE34 was a valid historical Nyx checkpoint: it crossed 10M cleanly at roughly 403 PGCR/sec and showed that the fixed 64-fetch, 34-PVE-write-lane profile avoided the worse DB/iowait cliff in that data band. It established DB/write coordination—not fetching or JSON decoding—as the immediate limiter, and it also proved ordinary restart recovery after a hard kill.

The later autonomy work superseded PVE34 as an operating prescription, not as evidence. Current-code alpha runs exceeded 1,000/sec and parser-owned S3 exceeded 2,000/sec while demonstrating that fetch, batch, and DB-lane settings must adapt to source and pressure conditions. Worker counts are now observations and learned priors rather than permanent identities.

The safe next experiment is a bounded, production-shaped alpha soak using learned priors and active telemetry, with reversible one-worker DB-lane trials and host memory/CPU pressure included in acceptance. Before any unattended extension, repeat hard-kill/normal-restart recovery and all integrity gates. This is proposed work; longer alpha soaks, beta downscale recovery, delta cadence, gamma lane tuning, rollup autotuning, and packaging the dirty worktree were still incomplete in the durable summary.

claims.value: The historical PVE34 10M-crossing run used 64 fetch workers with PVE/PVP/other DB lanes of 34/2/1, inserted 210,624 rows, and finished at 10.019M. It sustained about 403 PGCR/sec, averaged about 408/sec late, drained at about 372/sec, crossed 10M with zero parser errors, retries, duplicates, or terminal markers, and passed summary, sampled membership, S3, coverage, and protected-D2-Redis validation. Together with the same-band comparisons, this established PVE34 as the best practical fixed Nyx profile for that mostly-PVE band and identified DB/write coordination—with substantial idle headroom—as the limiter rather than fetch or JSON. It was a validated historical checkpoint, not a universal configuration.

The later durable autonomy evidence changed and superseded the fixed-profile operating model: current-code alpha proved more than 1,000 PGCR/sec (best clean fixed-ceiling alpha average 1083.1/sec, steady 1122.9/sec), parser-owned S3 reached 2141.3/sec average, beta latency correctly demanded more fetch capacity, and delta slow-edge correctly reduced fetch/retry to floor 4. The controller also reduced fetch below the former 112 fixation and recovered upward on genuine underfeed. Therefore PVE34 remains useful historical evidence about one DB-pressure shape, but its worker counts are no longer the parser’s identity: learned priors, measured pressure, scenario-specific reversible trials, and autonomous adaptation are the later operating model.
